candidateText:
The feed matters more than I expected. Rough sizing: 5,000 flights × 80 seats × ~80% load ≈ 320,000 passengers on the two routes; 20% connecting is ~64,000 people whose second leg rides on a healthy route. The four surviving routes run about 13–15% contribution margin on fares of roughly $130–150, so call it $20 of contribution per connecting leg — about $1.3M at risk.

Against $1.8M of losses avoided, exit nets closer to $0.5M. That's thin, and some of those connectors will rebook on the LCC and connect to us anyway, or we can interline. So exit is only clearly right if the aircraft go somewhere better.

On redeployment I'd want: unserved or underserved city pairs from the hub where no LCC flies, their estimated demand and achievable fare, plus whether the four healthy routes have spill — passengers we're turning away at peak times — that added frequency could capture.
said: I'll say that again — Air travel demand in Larkspur's cities has been roughly flat. An exhibit for you — Hub–Lakeport — Economics of one one-way flight, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($). Unserved or underserved city pairs from the hub where no LCC flies or data on whether passengers turned away at peak times — that's not something I have. I'll come back to the new routes' planning estimates shortly. What stands out to you in this exhibit?

Honestly, I think the structure is implied by the answer. Operating profit is revenue minus cost, and you've already told me the two things that matter: revenue dropped $24 million and load factor is flat. That means the revenue decline isn't seats, it's price per seat. And profit fell $24 million on exactly that revenue drop, which tells me cost is at best flat and probably up — so costs are the other half.

If you want it spelled out: price per ticket, seats flown, cost per seat split into fuel, labor, maintenance, airport fees. That's the whole tree. But I'd test price first because that's where the evidence already points.

One thing I would want — do we have fuel cost per gallon in FY2023 versus FY2025? That's usually the single biggest mover in an airline P&L.

I still think the recommendation stands: reprice up to recover the fare gap.

candidateText:
That settles it: at 30% lower cost per seat, the LCC can sustain today's fares and Larkspur can't. Matching is a permanent loss, and raising fares loses the passengers. So on those two routes there's no pricing path — it's an exit or restructure question.

Math on exiting both: Lakeport contributes ($1.2M) and Port Avery ($0.6M), so dropping them removes $1.8M of negative contribution. Fixed costs of $20M stay, at least initially. Operating profit goes from ($4M) to ($2.2M) — better, but still a loss. So exit alone doesn't get us to profit in 12 months; we'd also need to redeploy those 5,000 flights or shed fixed cost.

What I'd want: can the freed aircraft be redeployed to new destinations with no LCC presence, and what do the other four routes earn per flight as a benchmark? Also whether leases can be exited and how much fixed cost is genuinely avoidable.
said: I see. Your exit arithmetic is on the record. All nine aircraft are leased through 2030, so returning them early is not an option. Now, an exhibit: Proposed new routes — Planning estimates (average per flight across Hub–Ashford and Hub–Brookhaven). I'm afraid I don't have the competitor's frequency on those routes or results — revenue, contribution and flights — on the four non-contested routes to use as a benchmark for per-flight economics. Given the lease terms, what does that do to your exit option on Lakeport and Port Avery, and what would you do with the aircraft time instead?

candidateText:
Let me lay out how I'd approach this. We've got a $24M profit swing: revenue down $24M and costs roughly flat or up, so I want to size both sides.

On revenue: revenue equals routes × flights per route × 80 seats × load factor × average fare. Load factor is roughly unchanged, so the drop has to come from fewer flights flown or lower average fare per ticket — or mix shifting toward shorter, cheaper routes. I'd want fare and departure counts for FY23 vs FY25, by route if we have it.

On cost: split fixed (aircraft ownership, crew salaries, airport leases, overhead) from variable (fuel, landing fees, distribution). Fuel is usually the biggest single line for a regional, so I'd check price per gallon.

Can I get the revenue breakdown — departures and average fare for both years — plus the FY23 and FY25 cost lines?

candidateText:
The exhibit ties out: 60 passengers × $220 = $13,200 revenue, less $9,000 variable = $4,200 per flight × 2,000 = $8.4M in FY2023. FY2025: 60 × $140 = $8,400, less $9,000 = -$600 per flight × 2,000 = -$1.2M. So the entire $9.6M is the $80 fare cut: 60 pax × $80 × 2,000 flights = $9.6M, exactly.

Breakeven is $9,000 / 60 passengers = $150 revenue per passenger, so a $130 fare. At $120 we're below cash cost on every flight — we're paying to fly people.

On whether matching was right: no, not as a steady state. Matching only works if you can outlast the competitor, and we can't — their cost per seat is 30% lower, so the fare they're profitable at is structurally below our breakeven. We held load factor but bought it with money we don't have.

Do we know how much of our $9,000 variable cost is contractually fixed in the short run — specifically crew?
said: Right, the breakeven fare. The exhibit you have covers that: The Lakeport flight table has seats, load factor, fare, extras and each variable cost line for one flight in both years. Setting that aside, what are Larkspur's options on these two routes now that matching the fare is losing money on each flight, and which would you want to test first?
